title: Question 5
stem: A geostationary satellite orbits the Earth with a period of $24$ hours.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: the direction of the orbit about the Earth,
hints: Hint 1: Think about what geostationary means - the satellite stays fixed above the same point on Earth, so how must it move compared with the spinning Earth?
parts.proper_answer: west to east (same direction as Earth rotation).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Staying fixed means moving together**
Imagine standing on Earth watching the satellite. For it to appear stationary in your sky, it must drift around the Earth in step with you as Earth spins. Earth spins from west to east, so the satellite must travel the same way to keep up.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: the position of the satellite relative to the Earth's surface,
hints: Hint 1: Think about where a satellite must be so that its circular orbit keeps it over one fixed latitude as Earth turns underneath it.
parts.proper_answer: directly above the Equator (in the equatorial plane).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Only one line stays still**
If the satellite orbited over the poles or at an angle, Earth turning underneath would carry different places below it and it would appear to wander north-south. To stay over exactly the same spot, its orbit must be centred on Earth's centre and lie in the plane of the Equator, hovering above the Equator.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: a typical frequency for communication between the satellite and Earth.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what type of electromagnetic wave can pass easily through the atmosphere and be focused into a narrow beam by a dish - radio or light or somewhere in between?
parts.proper_answer: e.g. $6 \times 10^9\text{ Hz}$ (any value in microwave region, about $10^9$ to $3 \times 10^{11}\text{ Hz}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Microwaves for space links**
Satellite links use microwaves, typically a few GHz. These pass through the atmosphere with little absorption and can be beamed by dishes. A good typical value is a few $10^9\text{ Hz}$, for example $$f \approx 4 \times 10^9\text{ Hz to } 14 \times 10^9\text{ Hz}$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: A signal transmitted from Earth to a satellite has an initial power of $3.0\ \text{kW}$. The signal power received by the satellite is attenuated by $195\ \text{dB}$.
parts.text: Calculate the signal power received by the satellite.
hints: Hint 1: Start by recalling how gain in dB links the ratio of two powers using a base-10 logarithm.
Hint 2: Remember attenuation means the received power is smaller, so the dB value will be negative - set up the ratio of received power to the 3.0 kW transmitted power.
Hint 3: Rearrange to isolate the logarithm and then use powers of 10 to find the tiny received power, converting kW to W first.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The decibel rule for power**
For power, loss or gain in decibels compares output to input with a log: $$\text{gain/dB} = 10 \lg\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)$$ where $P_1 = 3.0\text{ kW} = 3000\text{ W}$ is transmitted and $P_2 = P$ is received.

Step 2: **Put in the -195 dB attenuation**
Attenuation is a negative gain: $$-195 = 10 \lg\left(\frac{P}{3000}\right)$$ So $$\lg\left(\frac{P}{3000}\right) = -19.5$$

Step 3: **Undo the log to find P**
Take antilog base 10: $$\frac{P}{3000} = 10^{-19.5}$$ $$P = 3000 \times 10^{-19.5} \approx 9.5 \times 10^{-17}\text{ W}$$ This extremely small power shows how much the signal spreads out and weakens over the huge distance to geostationary orbit.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: By reference to your answer in (i), explain why different frequencies are used for the up-link and the down-link in communication with the satellite.

markscheme_points.text: up-link has been (greatly) attenuated (before reachin or down-link signal must be (greatly) amplified (before t or up-link has (much) smaller intensity/power than down

hints: Hint 1: Compare the size of your answer in (b)(i) with the original 3.0 kW - what must the satellite do to this tiny received signal before sending it back down?
Hint 2: Think about what would happen at the receiver if the very weak incoming signal and the very strong outgoing signal used exactly the same frequency.
parts.proper_answer: The up-link signal arrives greatly attenuated / very weak and must be greatly amplified for the down-link. Different frequencies prevent the powerful down-link transmission from swamping / interfering with the weak up-link reception.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A tiny signal must be boosted**
Your answer in (i) is about $10^{-16}\text{ W}$, roughly $10^{19}$ times smaller than transmitted. The satellite receives this whisper of a signal and must amplify it enormously before re-transmitting it to Earth on the down-link.

Step 2: **Keep weak and strong apart**
If up-link and down-link shared the same frequency, the huge amplified down-link signal would drown out or swamp the tiny up-link signal being received at the same time. Using different frequencies keeps them separate so the receiver can pick out the weak one without interference.
